cards.title: Gene Amdahl
cards.body: IBM, Sunnyvale, April 1967. His paper promises a demonstration of "the continued validity of the single processor approach and of the weaknesses of the multiple processor approach in terms of application to real problems and their attendant irregularities." Three printed pages, one figure, no equations.
cards.prompt: Amdahl put a ceiling on parallel throughput without being told how many processors you had. What was the ceiling, and what set it?
cards.answer: Five to seven times the sequential processing rate. Data-management housekeeping runs 40% of executed instructions in production runs and is sequential, so it caps throughput "even if the housekeeping were done in a separate processor" — the processor count never enters the arithmetic.

cards.title: ILLIAC IV cut to one quadrant
cards.sub: 1972 · Burroughs / University of Illinois, on an ARPA contract
cards.body: Planned: 256 processors under central control, four quadrants of 64, targeting 10^9 instructions per second. Reported in the Proceedings of the IEEE, April 1972: "cost escalation and schedule delays" had cut the machine to one quadrant — 64 processors, about 200 million instructions per second. Burroughs built it; ARPA paid.
cards.prompt: One control unit drives all 64 of ILLIAC IV's processors. What happens to most of them the moment a program branches on its data?
cards.answer: They sit idle. One CU means one instruction stream, so every ALU is lock-stepped to the current instruction; a data-dependent branch only sets each PE's enable bit, and "only those PEs in an enabled state are able to execute the current instruction."

cards.title: "Validity of the Single Processor Approach…"
cards.sub: AFIPS Spring Joint Computer Conference, vol. 30, pp. 483–485
cards.body: AFIPS Conference Proceedings vol. 30, Spring Joint Computer Conference, Atlantic City, 18–20 April 1967, pages 483–485. DOI 10.1145/1465482.1465560. Reprinted in full in IEEE SSCS News, Summer 2007, which is the copy you can read free today.
cards.prompt: Amdahl's three pages are one item in a proceedings volume. Which talk is printed immediately before them, by whom, and why does the ordering matter?
cards.answer: Daniel Slotnick's "Unconventional systems", pages 477–481 of the same volume. Slotnick's name is on ILLIAC IV's own 1972 report in the Proceedings of the IEEE — the argument that bounds that whole class of machine is printed six pages after his talk.

cards.title: Amdahl's Law
cards.sub: 1967 → every capacity plan you will ever write
cards.body: The rule that outlived the machine: name the fraction of the work that must agree, and that fraction alone fixes the ceiling. The machine count never appears. It is why a stateless web tier scales, why one write master does not, and why "add servers" is a question, not a plan.
cards.prompt: Amdahl priced two processors with shared memory against one bigger machine. Give his three numbers, and say what the sharing cost.
cards.answer: About 2.2 times the hardware (the extra two tenths is the crossbar switching), performance about 1.8 once memory conflicts are counted, and so "a price performance degradation to 0.8 rather than an improvement to 2.0" for the single larger processor.
